Repeated cycles question the promise of lasting gain

Verse 3 asks what “profit” a person has from work. The word asks what is left over at the end. Verses 4–7 give four examples of motion with no gain. Generations, sun, wind, and rivers all return to where they began. Verse 9 draws the conclusion that nothing is new. Verse 11 adds that people forget what came before. “Under the sun” marks this as a report of life as observed.
Inheritance interrupts achievement

The Preacher finishes more than anyone before him (verse 9). Verse 18 names what spoils it. He must leave it all to the next man. Verse 19 says no one knows whether that heir will be wise or a fool. Verse 21 adds that the heir did not work for it. First Kings 12 shows Solomon’s son losing most of a kingdom. Verse 24 turns from gain to gift: enjoyment comes from God’s hand.
A list of times does not grant control

The poem in verses 1–8 lists fourteen pairs of times. People do not choose most of them. Birth, death, war, and loss arrive on their own schedule. Verse 11 names two gifts that pull against each other. Each thing is fitting in its time, and people sense something lasting. They still cannot see the whole work from start to finish. So verses 12–13 advise taking present good as a gift.
Observation exposes the limits of private advice

Verse 1 reports what the Preacher “saw.” He says twice that the oppressed had no comforter. Power stood on the side of those who harmed them. He offers no remedy and does not look away. Verses 9–12 give a partial answer on a small scale. A companion lifts the one who falls and keeps him warm. That is the comfort verse 1 found missing.
Words before God create obligations

Verses 1–2 set the scene: come to listen, and say little. A vow was freely made; no one had to make it (Deuteronomy 23:21–23). Verse 4 says that once spoken, it is owed. Verse 5 prefers no vow to a broken one. Verse 6 pictures a person telling the temple messenger it was a mistake. Words spoken before God have weight. The Preacher’s caution about speech runs through verses 3 and 7 as well.
Possession and enjoyment can separate

Chapter 5:19 said the power to enjoy wealth is a gift from God. Verse 2 shows a case where that gift is missing. The man has everything and tastes none of it. So having and enjoying are two separate things. A stranger ends up with what he gathered. Verse 9 commends being content with what is in front of you. The chapter ends in questions (verse 12) and gives no rule.
A funeral teaches what amusement can conceal

Verse 2 compares two houses. A feast lets people forget how life ends. A funeral shows “the end of all men.” The verse says the living should take that to heart. Its aim is clear sight, not gloom. Verse 14 adds that good days and bad days both come from God. Verse 15 reports a case that breaks the expected rule, as Job’s does.
Observed injustice strains a familiar rule

Verses 12–13 state what he knows: it goes well with those who fear God. Verse 14 states what he sees. Good people sometimes receive what bad people have earned. He sets the two statements side by side. He does not give up either one. Verse 11 notes what delayed justice does to those who watch. Verse 17 ends by admitting the limits of what anyone can find out.
Useful wisdom can remain unrecognized

The story in verses 14–15 takes three sentences. A great king besieges a small town. A poor man’s wisdom saves it. Then no one remembers him. His wisdom worked, and his reward failed. Verse 16 still says wisdom is better than strength. Its worth does not depend on being noticed.
Skill matters within a fragile world

Verses 8–9 say ordinary work carries risk. Digging, breaking walls, and cutting stone or wood can all injure. Verse 10 shows where wisdom helps. A sharpened ax needs less force. Preparing first saves strength later. The claim is modest: skill gives an advantage, not a guarantee. Verse 11 adds a case where help comes too late.
Uncertainty can become an excuse for inaction

Verse 4 pictures a farmer waiting for perfect weather. He watches the sky and never plants. The chapter says “you don’t know” four times (verses 2, 5, 6). The Preacher does not treat that as a reason to wait. He treats it as a reason to act widely. Give to seven or eight, and sow morning and evening. Uncertainty is an argument for doing more.
The ending places limits around learning

Verses 2–7 describe old age as a house falling into decline. In verses 9–10 the closing writer speaks about the Preacher. He praises him for weighing and arranging his sayings. Verse 11 compares wise words to goads and firmly set nails. Verse 12 warns that books have no end and study tires the body. An Egyptian scribe’s palette shows writing tools from that wider world. Verses 13–14 give the limit that matters: fear God, who judges every deed.
